title: The Crime at Gibeah
overview: In a time with no king, a Levite's journey home ends with his concubine gang raped and killed in an Israelite town, a crime that shocks all Israel.

parts.label: A wife leaves and is sought (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: In a time when Israel had no king, a Levite (from the tribe set apart for religious service) goes to Bethlehem to win back his concubine, a wife of lower legal standing, who had gone home to her father. The Hebrew says she was unfaithful, while early Greek and Aramaic versions say she was angry with him, so the reason she left is uncertain.

parts.label: Long delays, late start (vv. 4-15)
parts.note: Her father keeps pressing him to stay, and they finally leave late on the fifth day. The Levite refuses to stop at Jebus, later Jerusalem, because it was not an Israelite town, but in the Israelite town of Gibeah no one takes them in.

parts.label: An old man's welcome (vv. 16-21)
parts.note: An old man takes them home and feeds them. Like the Levite he is from the hill country of Ephraim, living in Gibeah among the local Benjamites, and many readers think his urgent warning not to sleep in the square shows he knew what the town was like.

parts.label: The mob at the door (vv. 22-24)
parts.note: Men of the town surround the house and demand the male guest so they can rape him, a scene that closely echoes the story of Sodom in Genesis 19. The host pleads his duty to protect a guest, yet offers his own daughter and the concubine instead.

parts.label: The woman is given up (vv. 25-28)
parts.note: When the men refuse to listen, the Levite seizes his concubine and sends her out to them, and they rape and abuse her all night; at dawn she falls at the door with her hands on the threshold. In the morning he tells her to get up, but she does not answer, and the Hebrew never says exactly when she died.

parts.label: A summons to the tribes (vv. 29-30)
parts.note: At home he cuts her body into twelve pieces and sends them throughout Israel, a shocking summons to act, like Saul's later call with pieces of oxen in 1 Samuel 11. People say nothing like this has happened since Israel left Egypt and urge one another to respond, which leads to the war in the next chapters.

disagreement: Readers differ on how the story judges the Levite: many older Christian interpreters saw him mainly as a wronged husband seeking justice, while many modern readers think the narrator is exposing his callousness as a sign of how far Israel had fallen.
think: The chapter ends with people urging each other to think it over and speak up; what do you think makes a community actually respond to a terrible wrong rather than only being shocked by it?
